title: Near-optimal quantum query lower bounds on bipartiteness and expansion testing in the bounded-degree graph model
authors: Chandrima Kayal, Sayantan Sen, Dániel Szabó
abstract: In this work, we study bipartiteness and expansion testing, two canonical problems in graph property testing in the bounded-degree model through the lens of quantum query complexity. In the classical setting, it is known that $\widetildeΘ(\sqrt{N})$ queries are necessary and sufficient for both these testing problems (Goldreich and Ron, 1999, 2000 & 2002), where $N$ denotes the number of vertices of the input graph. Due to their significance, (Ambainis, Childs, and Liu, 2011) initiated the study of these problems in the quantum setting and designed quantum algorithms for bipartiteness and expansion testing that perform $\widetilde{O}(N^{1/3})$ queries, showing a polynomial speedup. They also proved that $\widetildeΩ(N^{1/4})$ queries are necessary for expansion testing, but the possibility of an exponential quantum advantage for bipartiteness testing remained open. Despite significant effort, there has been no improvement in these results in the last decade and a half. In this work, we prove essentially tight $\widetildeΩ(N^{1/3})$ quantum query lower bounds for both bipartiteness and expansion testing, thereby completely characterizing the quantum query complexity of these problems up to polylogarithmic factors. While our proofs use the polynomial method similarly to Ambainis, Childs, and Liu, we use intermediate problems that we relate to the main problems via reductions, and perform a more precise analysis of the resulting polynomials, leading to the near-optimal lower bounds.
summary: This work rigorously determines the quantum query complexity for testing bipartiteness and expansion in bounded-degree graphs. By proving $\Omega(N^{1/3})$ lower bounds for both problems, the authors resolve long-standing open questions regarding quantum speedups for these fundamental graph properties. The methodology involves sophisticated algebraic techniques applied to quantum query complexity theory.
main_problem: The paper aims to establish near-optimal quantum query lower bounds for testing graph properties, specifically bipartiteness and expansion, within the bounded-degree graph model.
main_result: The authors prove essentially tight quantum query lower bounds of $\Omega(N^{1/3})$ for both bipartiteness and expansion testing, fully characterizing the quantum query complexity up to polylogarithmic factors.
method: The methodology employs the polynomial method, adapting techniques from previous work by relating the main problems to intermediate testing problems (like balancedness) via reductions and performing a precise analysis of the resulting polynomials.
model_or_system: The study focuses on graph theory problems (bipartiteness and expansion testing) applied to bounded-degree graphs, sometimes involving signed graphs where edges carry bit labels.
key_observables: Quantum query complexity ($q$), acceptance gap ($\Delta$), and the number of vertices ($N$).
important_parameters: The maximum degree of the graph, the error tolerance ($\epsilon$), and the size parameter $N$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on relating the true acceptance gap to a formal acceptance gap using polynomial approximations and bounding the error decay exponentially.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structure of 'yes' and 'no' instances for signed graphs, detail the reduction from balancedness testing to bipartiteness testing, and show the quantum circuit diagram for the testing oracle.
paper_structure: The paper builds from classical and quantum background results, develops the lower bound technique using the polynomial method on intermediate problems, proves the lower bounds for bipartiteness via reduction from balancedness, and establishes the bound for expansion testing.
why_interesting: While the topic is graph theory, the core technique—deriving complexity lower bounds using advanced polynomial methods and quantum query complexity—is highly relevant to understanding the limits of quantum algorithms in general.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: On the left, we have a yes instance balanced graph, and on the right, the no instance graph illustrates independent random edge signs. Theorem 3.3 shows that the no instance is far from balanced with high probability.

Fig. 2: We describe the reduction from balancedness testing to bipartiteness testing. On the left, the construction describes what happens when buv = 1 and on the right, it describes the reduction when buv = 0.

Fig. 4: The replacement graph construction. Each vertex u of the intermediate graph is replaced by a copy of Jc, whose color-j vertex is denoted (u, j). A color-j edge {u, v} becomes the external edge {(u, j), (v, j)}. The color-k edge illustrates that differently colored parallel intermediate edges use different neighbors. Only a few neighbors and internal cloud edges are shown schematically.

Figure 4 illustrates this standard replacement-graph construction. It has cN vertices and it is simple: different colors use different auxiliary vertices, even when two edges of different colors join the same pair of intermediate vertices. Every vertex has three internal neighbors and at most one external neighbor, so the maximum degree of this graph is four. Now we prove that if a graph H is an expander, then its corresponding replacement graph R(H) is an expander as well.

Fig. 5: A no instance before and after the replacement construction (in the non-overflow case). Only a few vertices, clouds, and edges are shown schematically; blue and red distinguish the two visible block classes, not matching colors.
